subsection: 9. Case study: race relations in France in the 1980s

notes.h: Background: the republican ideal and the politics of the 1980s
notes.b: To follow race relations in 1980s France you need the ideas and the politics behind them. France expected everyone to become French in the same way, and the party in power changed twice in the decade.
points: The republican ideal says citizens are individuals, equal before the law, so the state does not recognise ethnic or religious groups. This is why France expected migrants and their children to assimilate (adopt French language, values and civic culture) rather than keep a separate group identity.
Laïcité (state secularism, based on the 1905 law separating Church and State) keeps religion out of public institutions such as state schools. It was at stake in the headscarf affair of 1989.
Jus soli means nationality by birth in the territory. It matters here because French-born children of foreign parents could become French, and the Right tried to change how this worked in 1986-87.
Racism means ranking people by race and treating them differently, shown in violence, discrimination and exclusion.

Identity, here, is the question of how the second generation (French citizens of North African heritage) saw themselves and were seen. Cultural diversity means many cultures and religions in one society, which the banlieues and the second generation made visible.

Politically, the Socialist François Mitterrand became President in May 1981 and was re-elected in 1988. The Right won the 1986 parliamentary elections, giving a Chirac government (1986-88) that shared power with a Socialist president, known as cohabitation, and Michel Rocard led the Left's government from 1988.
notes.tip: Define assimilation, racism and identity precisely and then use them in your answer, rather than leaving them as a glossary. Examiners reward the terms applied to events, such as assimilation against integration in 1989.

notes.h: Background: the banlieues and the second generation
notes.b: By the early 1980s the children of North African and West African migrants lived in the banlieues, where unemployment and policing were the main grievances. Knowing who lived there, and why they were angry, explains the events that follow.
points: The banlieues were the working-class suburbs and high-rise estates around French cities. Many were built from the 1950s and 1960s to house migrant families and urban workers, and by the 1980s they had become rundown.
Many families lived in HLM estates (habitation à loyer modéré, public housing), so poor housing and the condition of the estates became part of the grievance.
Les Minguettes, an estate in Vénissieux near Lyon, was one of the best-known banlieues, and it became the scene of unrest in 1981.

The second generation, known as 'beurs' (verlan, a French slang that reverses syllables, from 'arabe'), had been born or raised in France and had French citizenship or a right to it. This is why their demand was to be treated as French.

The oil shock of 1973 ended the post-war economic boom, and migrant workers in the factories were among the first to lose their jobs. Youth unemployment in the banlieues was therefore far above the national average, and many young people were in low-skilled work or outside the labour market.
Relations between young people and the police were poor, and identity checks and stop-and-search practices were a constant complaint in the banlieues.

At the 1982 census about 800,000 Algerians lived in France, making them the largest foreign nationality, ahead of Portuguese and then Moroccans. Post-war labour migration, including from the Maghreb and West Africa, and the halt to labour migration in 1974 explain how these communities came to settle.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, say who the beurs were and why the banlieues were angry: unemployment and policing. Each correct, dated statement earns marks.

notes.h: The Minguettes unrest of 1981 and the Socialist response
notes.b: In summer 1981 anger in the banlieues erupted at Les Minguettes. The new Socialist government had to respond, and its measures helped some people but left the main grievances untouched.
points: In summer 1981 young men at Les Minguettes stole and burned cars, in what the press called 'rodéos', and clashed with police, drawing national television coverage.
The unrest spread to other banlieues in Lyon and elsewhere, and it drew national attention to the living conditions of second-generation migrants.
The Socialist government of François Mitterrand, elected in May 1981, responded with social programmes for the banlieues and promised reforms to immigration law.

The government created Priority Education Zones (ZEP, giving extra help to schools in deprived areas) in 1981 and launched the 'Banlieues 89' regeneration project in 1983. Both were limited in scale, so they did not remove the causes of disadvantage.

The Dubedout report of 1983 (by Hubert Dubedout, 'Ensemble, refaire la ville') recommended local regeneration and more involvement of residents in their neighbourhoods. It led to the 'développement social des quartiers' programme, so residents' views began to shape local projects.

The government regularised the status of about 130,000 undocumented migrants in 1981-82, so they could stay legally. A law of July 1984 created a ten-year residence card, which gave long-term security.

Mitterrand's 1981 manifesto promised local voting rights for foreign residents, and he spoke of a 'right to be different' (droit à la différence). The voting-rights promise was never carried out, which left a lasting grievance.
notes.tip: Date the unrest as summer 1981 and no other date. For cause and result, link the unrest to unemployment and policing, and the response to the new Socialist government.

notes.h: The March for Equality and against Racism, 1983
notes.b: The second generation organised a national protest in 1983. A police shooting set it off, and the march showed that beurs could run a national campaign.
points: The cause was the shooting and wounding of Toumi Djaïdja, a young man from Les Minguettes, by a police officer in June 1983. The priest Christian Delorme and the Protestant pastor Jean Costil helped organise the march.
The march set out from Marseille on 15 October 1983 with about 30 people. It grew as it crossed France and reached Paris on 3 December 1983 with tens of thousands of supporters.
A delegation was received at the Élysée (the presidential palace) by President Mitterrand, who promised the ten-year residence card. It was enacted in 1984.
The demands were equal treatment in jobs, housing and policing, and the right of second-generation migrants to be treated as French citizens.
The press called it the 'Marche des Beurs' because its core was second-generation young people, but its official title was the March for Equality and against Racism.
It was organised with local associations and churches, and it showed that second-generation migrants could run a national political campaign.
notes.tip: If asked why the march began, answer with the police shooting of Djaïdja in June 1983. Keep the March (autumn 1983, Marseille) separate from SOS Racisme (1984) and the 1985 concert.

notes.h: SOS Racisme and the anti-racist movement, 1984-85
notes.b: After the march, a new organisation turned anti-racism into a mass youth movement. It was popular and well backed, but critics doubted how much it changed.
points: SOS Racisme was founded in Paris in 1984, launched in October, by young activists including Harlem Désir and Julien Dray. It quickly grew into a national organisation with local branches.
Its slogan, 'Touche pas à mon pote' (Hands off my pal), appeared on a badge in the shape of a yellow open hand worn widely by young people. It expressed solidarity across ethnic lines.
It was supported by the Socialist government, by celebrities and by trade unions, and it ran concerts and campaigns against racism in schools and workplaces.
A free concert in the Place de la Concorde, Paris, on 15 June 1985 drew hundreds of thousands of young people, which shows how popular the movement had become.
Critics on the left argued that SOS Racisme focused on individual racism and did not address the social causes of disadvantage in the banlieues, such as unemployment and housing.
Some of the 1983 marchers accused the Socialists of using SOS Racisme to take over the anti-racist movement.
notes.tip: For why SOS Racisme took off, use the slogan and badge, the political and celebrity backing, and the concerts. Give 'hundreds of thousands' for the 1985 concert, not an exact number.

notes.h: The rise of the Front National, 1972-1984
notes.b: The Front National (FN) was a far-right party that won votes by campaigning against immigration. Its breakthrough in 1983 made it a political force.
points: The FN was founded on 5 October 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, born in 1928, a former paratrooper who had served in Algeria. It had the backing of far-right groups including Ordre Nouveau, and it drew on supporters of Algérie française (keeping Algeria French).
Its policies were to restrict immigration, expel illegal migrants and give 'national preference' (priority for French citizens) in jobs and housing.
Its breakthrough came in the municipal election at Dreux (Eure-et-Loir) in September 1983, not a by-election. Jean-Pierre Stirbois's list won about 17 per cent in the first round on 4 September.
In the second round on 11 September the FN joined a right-wing list that took the town. This ended the taboo on the mainstream Right allying with the FN.
In the 1984 European elections the FN won about 11 per cent of the vote and 10 seats, which confirmed that Dreux was not a one-off.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the elections: Dreux (September 1983, local), the 1984 European elections, the 1986 legislative elections and 1988. Call Dreux a municipal election.

notes.h: The rise of the Front National, 1986-1989
notes.b: The FN's national success followed. How many seats it won depended on the voting system as much as on its share of the vote, which is a point examiners like.
points: In the 1986 legislative elections, held under proportional representation (seats shared out according to each party's share of the vote), the FN won 35 seats in the National Assembly, with about 10 per cent of the vote.
The FN's support was strongest in the south and east of France, in areas with high unemployment and large migrant communities, such as Marseille and Nice.
In the April 1988 presidential election Le Pen won about 14.4 per cent of the first-round vote, about 4.4 million votes.
In June 1988 France had returned to single-member two-round constituency voting, which rewards parties that can win a majority locally, so the FN won only one seat.
Le Pen had been elected the youngest deputy in 1956, aged 27, for the Poujadist movement (a protest movement of small shopkeepers).
In September 1987 Le Pen said on radio that the Nazi gas chambers were 'a detail' of the history of the Second World War. The remark was widely condemned.
notes.tip: For why the FN gained votes, link it to unemployment and migrant communities in the south and east. The contrast between 35 seats in 1986 and one in 1988 is a good example of how the voting system matters.

notes.h: Government responses: the 1986 Pasqua laws and nationality
notes.b: When the Right won in 1986, policy turned towards control. Protests forced the government to retreat on nationality and a student's death forced it to drop a bill, and the Left then changed course in 1988.
points: The Chirac government of 1986-88, with Charles Pasqua as interior minister, passed laws that tightened immigration controls, permitted identity checks and made deportation easier.
The Pasqua law of September 1986 made expulsion of illegal immigrants easier and required visas for most foreigners, so entering France became harder.
On 25 October 1986 a charter flight deported about 100 Malians, an example of the tougher policy.

In 1986 the government planned to end the automatic acquisition of French nationality at 18 by French-born children of foreign parents, who would instead have to make a formal declaration. This was a change to jus soli in practice.

After mass protests, including from SOS Racisme, the plan was dropped in 1987 and a commission headed by Marceau Long was set up (1987-88). The Méhaignerie law of 1993 later introduced the declaration of will to acquire nationality.

Malik Oussekine died on 6 December 1986 after being beaten by riot police (the 'voltigeurs') during student protests against the Devaquet university reform bill. The outrage led the government to withdraw the bill.

When the Left returned in 1988, the Joxe law of 1989 (Pierre Joxe, interior minister) eased some of the 1986 restrictions. The Haut Conseil à l'intégration was created in December 1989, and the Rocard government preferred the word integration to assimilation.
notes.tip: Keep the laws apart: Pasqua (September 1986), the nationality plan (1986, dropped 1987), Joxe (1989) and Méhaignerie (1993). For why the nationality plan was dropped, say mass protest, including SOS Racisme. Chirac was prime minister; Mitterrand was president throughout.

notes.b: A dispute in one school became a national argument about what laïcité meant for Muslim pupils. The 1989 ruling and the later 2004 law show how the issue developed.
points: In autumn 1989 the headmaster, Ernest Chenière, of the Collège Gabriel-Havez in Creil (Oise), north of Paris, excluded three Muslim girls for wearing headscarves in class. It became a national controversy.

Education Minister Lionel Jospin asked the Conseil d'État (France's highest administrative court) for its opinion. On 27 November 1989 it ruled that headscarves were allowed unless ostentatious or used for pressure or propaganda.
Jospin's circular of 12 December 1989 told schools to apply that ruling and to accept headscarves unless they were ostentatious or used for proselytising.

The approach was case-by-case, not a ban, because each school judged whether a headscarf was ostentatious, and it lasted until the law of 15 March 2004 banned conspicuous religious symbols in state schools.
The affair showed the tension between laïcité and Muslim identity in schools, and it was debated in the press and by politicians of all parties.
notes.tip: Do not describe the 1989 ruling as a ban: it was case-by-case. Keep it apart from the 2004 law.

notes.h: The colonial past and Algeria in French race relations
notes.b: The 1980s tensions were not only about the 1980s. Decolonisation and the Algerian war (1954-62), which ended in Algerian independence, shaped who the migrants were, how others saw them, and which groups supported the FN.
points: Algerians had been French nationals before independence in 1962, and Algerian-origin families formed the largest group among the second generation. The Algerian war shaped how many French people saw North African migrants.
Many Algerian migrants and their children were linked by family and history to the war, and the harkis (Algerians who served France in the war) and their families remained a sensitive issue.

The Évian Accords (March 1962) led to independence, and between 800,000 and a million pieds-noirs (European settlers) left Algeria, mostly in 1962. Many settled in southern France, where the FN later won much of its support, though its voters were not only former settlers.
The FN drew support from Algerian war veterans and supporters of Algérie française, and its rhetoric echoed arguments about French identity from the colonial period.
Under the 'double jus soli' rule, a child born in France to a parent born in Algeria before independence was French at birth. This shows how the colonial past was written into the nationality rules.
The government's immigration policies in the 1980s were shaped by the memory of decolonisation, so debates about migrants were never only about the present.
notes.tip: Tie each 1980s event to the colonial past: the Algerian origin of the largest group, harkis and pieds-noirs, the FN's Algérie française roots and the nationality rules. A narrative without that link is weaker. Do not confuse beurs, harkis and pieds-noirs.

notes.b: Britain faced similar problems in the same years but answered them differently. The contrast comes from France's assimilationist model against Britain's multicultural framework.
points: Similarities: both countries had urban unrest and confrontations between police and young people in the early 1980s, and both had a far-right party that gained votes from anti-immigrant feeling.

France lacked the British framework of a series of Race Relations Acts (1965, 1968, 1976) and a public body like the Commission for Racial Equality. It did have the loi Pleven of 1972, which penalised racial incitement and discrimination.
France did not record ethnic statistics, which made discrimination harder to measure, for example in jobs or housing.
France's assimilation model treated citizens as individuals, so anti-discrimination arguments were framed in terms of universal rights rather than ethnic groups.
Britain answered its unrest of 1981 (the Brixton riots) with a public inquiry, the Scarman Report of 1981, while France's response was urban regeneration programmes such as Banlieues 89.
Britain's Commonwealth citizens had the vote, whereas non-citizen residents in France did not, which made the unfulfilled promise of local voting rights a live grievance.
notes.tip: Give a short paired list of similarities and differences with a named example on each side, such as Scarman against regeneration programmes, and say which country managed better and why. Do not claim France had no race law at all.

notes.h: Assessment: how France became multi-racial and how race relations developed
notes.b: A good judgement weighs what the second generation achieved against what stayed unresolved. State your view early and keep to it.
points: Achievement: the second generation found a national voice through the 1983 march and SOS Racisme, which made racism a public issue.
Limit: government responses centred on policing, immigration control and limited regeneration, so disadvantage in the banlieues persisted and remained a source of unrest.
Achievement: the Conseil d'État's 1989 ruling gave schools a legal framework for religious expression that lasted until 2004.
Limit: the FN's success showed that anti-immigrant politics could win mainstream attention, and mainstream parties were pulled towards some of its themes.

Contemporary views: assimilationists saw banlieue unrest as a failure of integration, while activists saw it as the result of racism and exclusion. Le Pen's supporters said immigration threatened French identity.
Contemporary government view: Socialist ministers presented integration, rather than assimilation, as the aim in 1989.
Later view: historians stress that the banlieues were shaped by housing policy, deindustrialisation and the colonial past, not by immigration alone.
notes.tip: For the Higher essay on how France became multi-racial, give the long-term causes briefly (decolonisation, labour migration, the Algerian war), then the 1980s events in date order: Minguettes 1981, the march 1983, SOS Racisme 1984, the FN 1983-88, Pasqua 1986, headscarves 1989.

keyTerms.definition: The belief that people can be ranked by race and treated differently on that basis, expressed in discrimination, violence and exclusion.
The expectation that migrants and their children adopt the language, values and civic culture of the French majority.
A person's sense of who they are, which for second-generation migrants could combine French citizenship with Algerian, Moroccan or Tunisian heritage.
The presence of many cultures, languages and religions within one society, which the banlieues and the second generation made visible in France.
The working-class suburbs and high-rise estates around French cities, where many migrant families lived from the 1960s.
The name given to the second generation of North African origin in France, derived from a verlan term for Arab.
The far-right party founded in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, which campaigned on immigration restriction and national preference.
The 1989 controversy over Muslim girls wearing headscarves in French schools, which led to a Conseil d'État ruling on laïcité.
The anti-racist organisation founded in 1984 by Harlem Désir and others, whose badge showed an open hand and the slogan 'Touche pas à mon pote'.
The French principle of state secularism, based on the 1905 law, which was at stake in the 1989 headscarf affair.
The principle that a child born in a country acquires its nationality, which French law applied in a limited way and which the right wished to restrict in 1986.
